task: Write the README for a small command-line tool. Use only these facts.
facts: The tool is called csv-dedupe.
It reads a CSV file and writes the rows to standard output with duplicates removed.
Two rows are duplicates when they have the same value in the key column, chosen with --key <column name>.
When duplicates are found, the first row is kept and the later ones are dropped.
Install it with: pipx install csv-dedupe
Example: csv-dedupe --key email customers.csv > unique.csv
It exits with code 2 and prints 'no such column' when the --key column isn't in the header.
It needs Python 3.11 or later.
questions: What is the tool for?
What do you run first to install it?
How do you know which row is kept when there are duplicates?
What happens if you pass a --key column that doesn't exist?

task: Write a runbook for restoring the nightly database backup, for an on-call engineer. Use only these facts.
facts: The backup job runs every night at 02:00 UTC and writes an archive named db-YYYY-MM-DD.tar.zst to the backups bucket.
Restoring needs shell access to the database host and membership of the db-admins group.
First stop the app with: systemctl stop app
Restore with: backup restore --date YYYY-MM-DD --target /srv/db
A successful restore prints 'restored N tables' and exits 0.
Then start the app with: systemctl start app, and check that /health returns 200.
If the restore prints 'archive not found', run backup list to see which dates exist; archives are kept for 7 days.
If the restore fails for any other reason, page the database owner and don't retry more than once.
questions: What is this runbook for, and who can follow it?
What must you do before running the restore command?
How do you know the restore worked?
What do you do if the restore prints 'archive not found'?

task: Write an architecture decision record for this decision. Use only these facts.
facts: The decision: move the background job queue from Redis to Postgres, using SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.
It was decided on 2026-10-10 by the platform team.
Redis was used only for the queue; everything else already lives in Postgres.
Dropping Redis removes one service to run, patch and monitor.
Postgres handled 400 jobs per second in a load test, and the peak load is 60 jobs per second.
Downside: job polling adds load to the main database.
Rejected option: keep Redis and add persistence, because it still leaves two stores to back up.
Revisit if the peak load passes 200 jobs per second.
questions: What was decided, and when?
Why was Postgres chosen over Redis?
What is the main downside?
When should the decision be revisited?

task: Rewrite this how-to guide so a reader can follow it without help. Keep every command, value, step and instruction for using it; the history and filler may be cut.
facts: Adding a tenant needs the billing-admin role.
Step 1: billing tenant create --name <name>
Step 2: billing plan set --tenant <name> --plan <plan>, where plan is starter, team or enterprise.
Step 3: billing sync --tenant <name>
The sync prints 'synced' when it works.
If the sync prints 'plan missing', set the plan and run the sync again.
draft:
# Tenants

Tenants are a core concept of the billing service and have been since the 2024 redesign, when we moved away from per-account billing. There are many considerations around tenants. Basically, to add one you'll want to make sure you have the billing-admin role, and then it's worth noting that you need to create the tenant row (billing tenant create --name <name>), and you need to set the plan with billing plan set --tenant <name> --plan <plan>, where plan is starter, team or enterprise. Then the sync job has to run: billing sync --tenant <name>. The sync prints 'synced' when it works. If it says 'plan missing', the plan step was skipped, so set the plan and run the sync again.
questions: What does this guide help you do?
What do you need before you start?
How do you know it worked?
What do you do if the sync says 'plan missing'?

task: Rewrite this README so a newcomer can get the tool running first. Keep every command, path, value and instruction for using it; the history and philosophy may be shortened or cut.
facts: Install with: cargo install logtail
Stream a file with: logtail --follow /var/log/app.log
Lines matching --grep <pattern> are highlighted.
The config file is optional and lives at ~/.config/logtail/config.toml.
On 'permission denied', run it as a user in the adm group.
draft:
# logtail

## History

logtail started in 2023 as a weekend project to replace a pile of shell scripts that tailed log files on several servers. Over time it grew a plugin system and a config format. In 2025 the config moved from INI to TOML.

## Philosophy

We believe logs should be easy to read. The project values small, fast tools.

## Getting it

You can install logtail with: cargo install logtail. Then run logtail --follow /var/log/app.log to stream a file. Lines matching --grep <pattern> are highlighted. The config file lives at ~/.config/logtail/config.toml and is optional. If you see 'permission denied', run it as a user in the adm group.

What do you run first to install and try it?
Where does the config file live, and do you need one?

task: Rewrite these release notes so a user knows what changed and what they must do. Keep every change, value and instruction; promotional wording may be cut.
facts: Version 2.4.
Exports are about three times faster.
The --legacy flag was removed; scripts that pass it must drop it, and its behaviour is now the default.
All dates are now ISO 8601, such as 2026-10-16 instead of 10/16/2026, which can break anything that parses the CSV output.
Fixed: exports with more than 65,536 rows were cut short.
draft:
# v2.4

We're thrilled to announce v2.4, a robust release packed with improvements! We've been hard at work refactoring the export pipeline, which is now seamlessly faster (about three times). Also, the --legacy flag has been removed, so scripts using it will need to drop it; its behaviour is now the default anyway. Dates everywhere are now ISO 8601 (2026-10-16 instead of 10/16/2026), which may affect anything parsing our CSV output. Finally, we fixed the bug where exports with more than 65,536 rows were cut short.
